row.prior_work: BrainBench (Luo et al. 2024, *Nature Human Behaviour*, arXiv 2403.03230, v4 HTML re-read 2026-11-05): LLMs averaged 81.4% against 63.4% for experts, "scored as choosing the abstract with the lower perplexity"; "Chat or instruction-optimized models performed worse than their base model counterparts"; the authors avoided prompting because "Prompting in natural language may yield less reliable judgments"; the best single model in the text, Phi-3, scored 82.5%. They test no valence, flattery or option-order shortcut. No paper reports a prompted Claude model, or a valence question, on BrainBench (web search "BrainBench Claude Opus prompted accuracy neuroscience results prediction frontier models", 2026-11-05: none). Predicts: unknown. **What this bet adds:** ss-b10c's 41-item Opus secondary completed to all 200 items, read against the stricter published LLM figure (81.4%) rather than the experts', with the forecasting prompt on the same items as the matched comparison.

row.premortem: If this fails, the most likely reason is that Haiku's averaged accuracy moves more than 5 points from 76.2% under the new wording, because its position-driven picks are near 0.5 on half its items.
row.prior_work: Prompt-paraphrase work predicts some movement and disagrees on how much. Mizrahi et al. 2024 (*TACL*, arXiv 2401.00595, abstract opened 2026-11-05) find single-instruction results brittle across 6.5M instances, 20 LLMs and 39 tasks. Sclar et al. 2023 (arXiv 2310.11324, abstract) report "performance differences of up to 76 accuracy points" on LLaMA-2-13B from formatting alone, few-shot. arXiv 2509.01790 ("Flaw or Artifact?", abstract; 7 LLMs including GPT and Gemini, 6 benchmarks, 12 paraphrased templates) finds that "much of the prompt sensitivity stems from heuristic evaluation methods", and that with LLM judges the variance drops substantially. None tests a valence question, BrainBench or a Claude 5 model; our answers are structured probabilities, not matched strings, which is the setting 2509.01790 finds more robust. Predicts: mixed. **What this bet adds:** the first paraphrase test of ss-b10c's shortcut, item by item against its first wording, on the two models that carried its rule.
